newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia budget seen tackling wealth gap.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia budget seen tackling wealth gap.

text.p: Indonesia's state budget aims to ease a growing wealth gap through increased spending on poor eastern parts of the sprawling archipelago, analysts said on Tuesday.

"It's a business-as-usual budget that aims to underline macro-economic stability," economist Mari Pangestu of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said of the measures unveiled by President Suharto on Monday.

The budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting in April allocated 38.9 trillion rupiah ($16.5 billion) for development, up 12.8 percent from 1996/97. Suharto said the increase was aimed partly at freeing Indonesians "trapped in pockets of poverty".
"We still have the problem of gaps between sectors, between regions and between groups in society," Suharto said on Monday.
"We have been able to address them in stages and with planning, and it has started to produce some results," he said.
Based on a 1996 national survey, the number of people below the poverty line had fallen to around 22 million, or about 11 percent of the population, in 1996 from 26 million in 1993.
A person who earns less than 50 U.S. cents a day is considered to be below the poverty line in Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country with some 200 million people.

"There's been resentment in the outer regions that nothing can be done without the approval of Jakarta, and the increased emphasis now in eastern Indonesia seems to be a recognition of this," a foreign political analyst said.
"There is an attempt to redress the situation, and maintain the government's support in these regions (during general elections on May 29)," he said.

Suharto said 11 areas of economic growth potential would be developed in eastern Indonesia, which has long been shunned by foreign investors because of the lack of infrastructure and other facilities.
Analysts said two riots in as many weeks in different parts of Indonesia reflected ethnic and religious tensions rooted in economic and social gaps.
While Indonesia's impressive economic performance had benefited the business community, analysts say the effects have yet to trickle down to the poor.
Foreign Minister Ali Alatas on Monday acknowledged the growing gap between rich and poor but added that this was inevitable as a country develops its economy and industry.
"We are talking about it very openly in Indonesian society," he said.
The government was well aware of the problems and was working to remedy them, he said, adding that they should not be blown out of proportion.
The head of the World Bank in Indonesia, Dennis de Tray, gave the budget a thumbs-up, saying it exercised fiscal discipline despite it being an election year.
"I would be hard-pressed to find another country that had the fiscal discipline to bring in quite a tight public sector budget in an election year," he said.
